Hardware bound for the Moon and Mars is rehearsed on Earth first. Most of the places we rehearse in were never measured against where they stand in for.

Eidolon finds the closest double on Earth for any site you plan to land.

Eidolon

A planning tool for terrestrial analog sites. Pick a landing site on the Moon or Mars and Eidolon ranks the places on Earth that come closest to it.

Built for
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
Challenge
Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
Data
NASA and partner agency open data. Imagery, terrain and match scores in this preview are placeholders.

Every rover, drill and habitat bound for the Moon or Mars rehearses on Earth first. Eidolon finds where.

How it works

  1. Pick a sitePin any point on the Moon or Mars, or start from a candidate base location.
  2. Characterise itTerrain, slope, roughness and surface brightness are read from orbital data around the pin.
  3. Find its doublesEarth sites are ranked by how closely they match, then compared side by side, with a weather window for field tests.

Beyond the Moon and Mars

Venus, Mercury and the outer moons need habitats Earth can only partly stage. They come online here as our reach and our tech grow.

Venus

Cloud cities

At about 50 km up, the air is near 1 bar and around 75 °C. Habitats float in the clouds instead of landing, as in NASA's HAVOC study.

Concept
Mercury

Polar mines

Permanently shadowed craters near the poles hold water ice, a short walk from a 430 °C day. Ice and metals for everything that comes after.

Concept
Callisto, Jupiter

Low-radiation base

Far enough out to miss Jupiter's worst radiation. NASA's HOPE study picked it as the site for a crewed outpost in the Jupiter system.

Concept
Titan, Saturn

Shoreline habitat

Nitrogen air at 1.5 bar and seas of liquid methane. No pressure suit needed, only warmth and oxygen at −179 °C.
